analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve every new federal regulation and lets existing ones expire.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, no new federal regulation could take effect unless both chambers of Congress passed a law specifically approving it within 70 legislative days; if Congress did nothing, the rule would die and could not be reissued in the same form. It would also phase out every federal regulation already in effect over ten years: each year agencies would have to submit 10% of their rules for review, and any rule Congress did not affirmatively extend would terminate. Presidents could exempt emergency, criminal-law, national-security, and trade-agreement rules for limited periods.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by federal rules — energy, manufacturing, finance, agriculture, pharmaceuticals — would gain the most, because most new rules would never survive a vote in both chambers and most existing rules would eventually lapse without an affirmative act of Congress. Congress itself would gain sweeping power over the executive branch.

how_it_helps.text: No new regulation could take effect unless both the House and Senate enact a joint resolution approving it within 70 legislative days; if Congress fails to act, the rule is deemed not approved and cannot be reissued in substantially the same form without new authorizing legislation.

Every rule already in effect when the bill becomes law would be phased out: each agency must designate at least 10% of its existing rules for review annually for ten years, and any rule not extended by Congress within that window terminates.
Regulations would expire ten years after congressional approval unless Congress affirmatively extends them, and rules could not simply be reissued in the same form afterward.

The President could exempt rules from these requirements for limited periods if they address an imminent health or safety threat, enforce criminal law, involve national security, or implement a trade agreement; Federal Reserve monetary policy is excluded entirely.
Proponents' stated rationale is accountability: agencies currently issue binding rules without a vote of Congress, and this would return that lawmaking power to elected legislators.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost: virtually every federal protection delivered through regulation — clean air and water limits, food and drug safety, workplace safety, vehicle standards, and consumer financial protections — would need an act of Congress to take effect or to survive, and history shows Congress rarely passes laws on individual rules. The practical result would be that most protections lapse or never start.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal safety rules

drawbacks.text: The mechanism defaults to inaction: because Congress would have to pass a separate joint resolution for each rule within 70 legislative days, and hundreds of rules are issued each year, the overwhelming majority would fail by default — a design that functions as a near-universal moratorium on regulation rather than genuine oversight.

Rules protecting public health and safety could be delayed up to 90 days by presidential determination even in emergencies, but no rule could take effect without a full vote of both chambers, leaving gaps in protections while Congress debates.

The bill carves out rules of 'particular applicability' — including those approving corporate or financial structures, mergers, and rates — from the approval requirement entirely, meaning some economically significant agency decisions face less scrutiny than broad public-interest rules.

A good-faith supporter would acknowledge the accountability argument has force — Congress does delegate broad lawmaking power to agencies — but the remedy here applies the same burdensome approval process to routine technical rules and to landmark protections alike, and would be all but impossible to administer at scale.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core idea — that elected lawmakers should answer for rules that carry the force of law — is a real and respectable concern. But the design is not a workable version of it: requiring an affirmative act of Congress for every rule, with death by default, would shut down the regulatory system that enforces nearly every health, safety, and consumer protection the federal government provides. The costs to ordinary people overwhelmingly outweigh the accountability gain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Rules Committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee in March 2019, and neither committee ever acted on it; it sat until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King (R-IA) introduced the Sunset Act of 2019 on January 30, 2019.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Rules Committee on the day of introduction.
On March 25, 2019, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law.
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and consumer regulations came out ahead, because the bill's default-death mechanism would have gutted most of those protections had it become law; regulated industries did not get the near-automatic regulatory relief they would have gained from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on federal regulations

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party; no votes were ever taken, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals, agriculture)
industries.note: The bill would let most existing regulations expire and make new ones nearly impossible to enact, cutting compliance costs for regulated firms. Those rules are what enforce air and water quality, food and drug safety, workplace protections, and consumer financial safeguards, so the industry's gain comes at the public's expense.

industries.industry: Companies subject to rules of particular applicability (utility rates, corporate and financial structures, mergers)
industries.note: The bill exempts rules approving corporate or financial structures, mergers, and rates from the congressional approval requirement, so those industry-specific agency decisions would be spared the process that applies to general public-interest rules.
